fields.summary: Pilate and Herod find no guilt in Jesus, but the crowd asks for Barabbas, and Jesus is crucified at the Skull between two criminals, promising one of them paradise. Darkness falls, Jesus dies, and Joseph of Arimathea lays the body in a tomb.

fields.title: Luke 24
fields.body_html:
1Very early on the first day of the week, at the first light of dawn, the women came to the tomb. They brought with them the spices they had made ready. 2They found that the stone had been rolled back from the tomb. 3But when they went inside, they found no body there. 4They were at a loss to know what this meant. Then two men were standing by them, their clothing flashing with light. 5The women were terrified and kept their faces bowed to the ground. But the men said to them, “Why are you looking among the dead for the one who is alive? 6He is not here; he has been raised. Remember what he told you when he was still in Galilee. 7He said that the Son of Man had to be handed over to sinful people and be crucified, and on the third day rise again.” 8Then his words came back to them. 9They went back from the tomb and reported all of this to the Eleven and to everyone else. 10The women were Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the others who were with them. They kept telling the apostles about these things. 11But to the apostles the report sounded like nonsense, and they would not believe the women.

12Peter, though, got up and ran to the tomb. He bent down to look in and saw nothing but the linen wrappings. Then he went home, amazed at what had taken place.

Two disciples walk to Emmaus

13On that very day two of them were walking to Emmaus, a village about seven miles from Jerusalem. 14They were deep in conversation about all that had happened. 15While they were talking it over and debating, Jesus himself came near and began to walk with them. 16But their eyes were held back, and they did not know him. 17He said to them, “What is this conversation you are having with each other as you walk?” They stopped walking, and their faces were gloomy. 18One of them, a man named Cleopas, answered him, “Can you be the one visitor in Jerusalem who has not heard what has gone on there in the past few days?” 19“What things?” he asked them. They said to him, “About Jesus from Nazareth. He was a prophet, a man whose deeds and words had great power in the eyes of God and of all the people. 20And our chief priests and leaders handed him over to be condemned to death, and they crucified him. 21Our hope was that he was the one who would redeem Israel. And on top of all that, this is now the third day since it happened. 22And then some women of our company gave us a shock. They went to the tomb at first light 23and found that his body was gone. They came back and said they had even seen angels in a vision, angels who say that he is alive. 24Some of our people went to the tomb as well. They found everything the way the women had described it, but they saw nothing of him.” 25Then he said to them, “You are without understanding, and your hearts are slow to believe all that the prophets said! 26Christ had to suffer these things and enter into his glory, did he not?” 27Then, starting with Moses and going on through all the prophets, he explained to them what was written about himself in every part of the Scriptures.

28They came near the village they were heading for, and he gave the impression of going on farther. 29But they would not let him go on. “Stay with us,” they said. “Evening is coming, and the daylight is already fading.” He went inside to stay with them. 30When he had taken his place at the table with them, he took the bread and said the blessing. Then he broke it and handed it to them. 31Then their eyes were opened and they knew who he was. And he could no longer be seen. 32They said to each other, “Did we not feel our hearts on fire inside us while he talked with us on the road and laid the Scriptures open to us?” 33Without delay they got up and went back to Jerusalem. They found the Eleven gathered with their companions, 34who were saying, “The Lord has truly been raised, and he has appeared to Simon!” 35The two then told their own story: what took place on the road, and how he became known to them in the breaking of the bread.

Flesh and bones

36As they were talking about all this, Jesus himself was standing among them. 37But they were alarmed and filled with fear, for they thought they were looking at a spirit. 38He said to them, “Why are you so shaken? Why are these doubts coming up in your hearts? 39Look at my hands and my feet, and see that it is really I. Feel me and see. Spirits have no flesh and bones; you can see that I do.” 40After saying this, he let them see his hands and feet. 41Their joy and amazement were so great that they still could not believe it. Then he asked them, “Do you have something here to eat?” 42They handed him a piece of grilled fish. 43He took it and ate it while they watched.

Everything written about him

44Then he said to them, “This is what I was telling you when I was still with you: whatever the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms have written about me must be fulfilled.” 45Then he opened their minds to make sense of the Scriptures. 46He told them, “This is what stands written: Christ is to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, 47and in his name repentance and the forgiveness of sins are to be announced to all the nations, starting from Jerusalem. 48You are witnesses to these things. 49I am sending upon you what my Father promised. As for you, remain here in the city until power from on high clothes you.”

Blessing at Bethany

50He led them out until they were near Bethany. There he raised his hands and blessed them. 51He was still blessing them when he parted from them and was borne up into heaven. 52They bowed down in worship before him, then made their way back to Jerusalem with great joy. 53And they spent all their time in the temple, blessing God.
fields.summary: Women find the tomb empty and are told that Jesus has been raised. The risen Jesus walks with two disciples to Emmaus, appears to the others with flesh and bones, opens the Scriptures to them, and is taken up near Bethany.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
He led them out until they were near Bethany. There he raised his hands and blessed them. He was still blessing them when he parted from them and was borne up into heaven. They bowed down in worship before him, then made their way back to Jerusalem with great joy. And they spent all their time in the temple, blessing God.

— Luke 24:50–53

Luke’s Gospel ends where it began, in the temple, with people praising God. In the first chapter an old priest came out of the sanctuary unable to speak, and could not give the blessing the people were waiting for. In the last chapter Jesus lifts his hands and blesses his disciples, and they go back to the temple full of joy. The blessing Zechariah could not give has been given.

The question the book leaves with you

Luke is full of people who are found: shepherds, a widow, a sinful woman, a Samaritan leper, a chief tax collector up a tree, a criminal on a cross. And it is full of people who must decide whether to come in. The clearest of them is the elder brother in the parable of the lost son. His father comes out to plead with him, and says:

His father answered, ‘My child, you are with me always, and all that is mine belongs to you. But it was only right to celebrate and rejoice, for this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.’”

— Luke 15:31–32

Jesus does not tell us whether he went in. The story was told to people who grumbled that Jesus welcomed sinners, and it leaves them, and us, standing at the door of the feast. Luke’s Gospel is good news for the lost. But it asks those who think they were never lost whether they will rejoice when others are found.

The two on the road to Emmaus leave another question. They walked beside the risen Jesus for seven miles and did not know him. Their hearts burned as he opened the Scriptures, and their eyes were opened when he broke the bread. Luke wrote, perhaps, for readers who would never see Jesus as the apostles did. He tells them where he is to be found: in the Scriptures opened, at the table, among those who gather in his name.

Where the book points

It points, first, to Jerusalem and beyond. The risen Jesus tells his disciples that repentance and the forgiveness of sins are to be announced in his name “to all the nations, starting from Jerusalem.” They are to wait in the city until power from on high clothes them. Luke’s Gospel is the first of two volumes, and the second, the Acts of the Apostles, begins with that promise kept and follows the message from Jerusalem to Rome.

It points, second, to a way of life. The Jesus of Luke’s Gospel eats with outcasts, notices widows, warns the rich and prays all night. He tells his followers to pick up their cross “every day”, to show compassion as their Father shows compassion, and to go and do as the Samaritan did. To read Luke and not be changed in how we treat the poor and the outsider is not really to have read it.

And it points to joy. The book that begins with an angel announcing “a great joy that is for all the people” ends with disciples going home “with great joy”. Between them stand a shepherd carrying a lost sheep home on his shoulders, a woman calling her neighbours to celebrate a coin, and a father running down the road.

Where to go from here

Luke’s stories have been preached more than almost any others in the Bible, and many of the best sermons on them are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On the birth of Jesus (chapter 2). Martin Luther’s The Story of the Birth of Jesus (2:1–14) and John Newton’s The Angel’s Message and Song (2:8–14).
  • On Martha and Mary (10:38–42). Augustine of Hippo’s sermon Martha and Mary.
  • On prayer. Andrew Murray’s With Christ in the School of Prayer, which begins with the disciples’ request, “Lord, teach us how to pray” (11:1), and J. C. Ryle’s Do You Pray? (18:1).
  • On the great invitation (chapter 14). Charles H. Spurgeon’s Compel Them to Come In (14:23).
  • On the lost son (chapter 15). Alexander Maclaren’s The Prodigal and His Father (15:11–24), and Frederick W. Robertson’s The Prodigal and His Brother (15:11–32), which gives the elder brother his due.
  • On money (chapter 16). John Wesley’s The Use of Money (16:9).
  • On the tears of Jesus (19:41–42). Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s The Saviour’s Tears over the Lost.
  • On the cross. D. L. Moody’s The Dying Thief (23:39–43).
  • On the risen Lord (chapter 24). Andrew Murray’s Jesus Himself, on the two disciples whose eyes were opened (24:31), and John Bunyan’s The Jerusalem Sinner Saved, on the command to preach “starting from Jerusalem” (24:47).

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Luke in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this Gospel.

But the best next step is the one Luke himself intended. Turn the page to his second book, the Acts of the Apostles, and watch what happened when the promise of the Father came. And then come back to the first, and read it again, listening for the word that runs all through it, today: the day of the Saviour’s birth, the day salvation came to Zacchaeus’s house, and the day Jesus promised to the man dying beside him. It is meant for you too:

Jesus answered him, “Truly I tell you, this very day you will be with me in paradise.”

— Luke 23:43
